meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Money cannot buy health, but I'd settle for a diamond-studded wheelchair'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it only to a 1959 English newspaper filler crediting Parker. Tentatively hers, but no primary source. Attributed, not verified.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic & Algonquin Round Table wit
answer.sourceLine: Printed under Parker’s name since at least January 1959 — inside her lifetime, and with no rival claimant — but no letter, essay, interview or book of hers has ever been produced containing it. Quote Investigator ↗, which traced the citations, goes no further than saying the line “should be tentatively credited to Dorothy Parker.”

source.excerpt: Money can’t buy health. but I’d settle for a diamond-studded wheelchair. —Dorothy Parker.
trail: 5 January 1959 — the earliest appearance anyone has found is a filler line in the Liverpool Echo’s “Echoes and Gossip of the Day” column, headed “Settling Up,” already crediting Dorothy Parker and giving no source of its own. A second English paper, the Nantwich Guardian, ran it on 19 February 1959 (Quote Investigator ↗).

1968 — Evan Esar filed the line under “Health and Wealth” in 20,000 Quips and Quotes, in the now-standard “Money cannot buy health” wording, which carried it into a generation of quotation books; The Portable Curmudgeon reprinted it with the Parker credit in 1987 (Quote Investigator ↗).

2004 — Barry Day placed the line in Dorothy Parker in Her Own Words ↗ beside a genuine 1956 Paris Review remark; Quote Investigator notes the wheelchair line does not occur in that interview and that no supporting citation is given.

Still missing — Parker died in 1967, so the 1959 printings fall inside her lifetime, yet no letter, essay, interview or book of hers has ever been produced containing the line, and Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page ↗ does not list it in any section.
source.excerptNote: As reproduced by Quote Investigator from the Liverpool Echo of 5 January 1959, under the sub-heading “Settling Up” — a one-line filler with no occasion, no interviewer and no source; the stray full stop after “health” is in the transcription. The familiar modern form, “Money cannot buy health,” is the one Evan Esar printed in 1968.
source.rightsNote: No work of Parker’s has been shown to contain this sentence, so there is no first publication to date and no copyright status that can honestly be asserted. Its earliest known printing is an unsourced one-line filler in a British newspaper of 5 January 1959, which establishes circulation rather than authorship; quotle.info therefore records the wording’s rights status as undetermined rather than claiming it as public domain.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: Dorothy Parker
author.bio: Born Dorothy Rothschild in Long Branch, New Jersey, Parker became a theatre critic for Vanity Fair in 1918 and a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, the lunch circle whose wisecracks were syndicated across America. Her poetry collection Enough Rope (1926) was a bestseller, and she went on to write short stories, New Yorker criticism and Hollywood screenplays, earning two Academy Award nominations before being placed on the Hollywood blacklist. Being the most quotable woman of her generation is exactly why lines she never wrote keep arriving under her name.

misattribution.heading: What gets claimed — and what holds
misattribution.intro: No rival claimant has ever surfaced — Quote Investigator found no plausible alternative attribution — so this is not a case of the wrong name on the right line. The problem is the certainty around it: quotation collections present it as settled Parker, and two specific habits of transmission have quietly manufactured a provenance it does not have.

items.why: The earliest printing — the Liverpool Echo of 5 January 1959 — uses the contraction: “Money can’t buy health.” (Quote Investigator does not reproduce the Nantwich Guardian’s wording.) The formal “cannot” that circulates today is the wording Evan Esar printed in 20,000 Quips and Quotes in 1968, and it is that later version the quote sites reproduce (Quote Investigator ↗).

Barry Day’s 2004 Dorothy Parker in Her Own Words sets the line next to a genuine 1956 Paris Review answer from Parker, which invites readers to treat the interview as its source. Quote Investigator notes the wheelchair line does not occur in that interview, and that Day supplies no citation for it (Quote Investigator ↗).

Quotation sites print it as fact. The specialists do not: Quote Investigator concluded only that the saying “should be tentatively credited to Dorothy Parker” (Quote Investigator ↗), and Wikiquote’s Parker page ↗ does not list the line at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position is the one Quote Investigator reached: two English newspapers were crediting Parker with the joke by early 1959, within her lifetime and with no competing claimant, so it should be tentatively credited to her — but nothing she is known to have written or said contains it. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it sounds exactly like her
lead: The joke is built the way Parker’s best one-liners are built: set up a pious platitude, then refuse to be improved by it. “Money cannot buy health” is the sort of thing that belongs on a hospital wall; the diamond-studded wheelchair is the Algonquin table’s answer to it. That structural fit is genuinely part of the evidence — but it is also precisely why unattached jokes drift toward famous wits in the first place.

What the paper trail actually shows is thinner than the confidence of the quote sites. The two earliest printings anyone has found are both filler items in English regional newspapers — the Liverpool Echo on 5 January 1959 and the Nantwich Guardian on 19 February 1959 — each crediting Parker, neither saying where or when she said it. That is the classic profile of a line already circulating by word of mouth before it reached print, which makes the original occasion very hard to recover.
context.detailsSummary: How the modern wording took hold
detailsBody: The earliest printing, the Liverpool Echo of 5 January 1959, uses the contraction: “Money can’t buy health.” (Quote Investigator does not reproduce the Nantwich Guardian’s wording.) The formal “Money cannot buy health” that dominates today is the version quotation-collector Evan Esar filed under “Health and Wealth” in 20,000 Quips and Quotes in 1968, and that is the form later collections reproduce — The Kansas City Times in 1977, The Portable Curmudgeon in 1987, and onward, all per Quote Investigator ↗.

Quote Investigator also records the image escaping Parker altogether: a 1974 Circus magazine piece on the band Brownsville Station has members saying they would not mind being paralysed in a car wreck “as long as I can go in a diamond-studded wheelchair.” A good joke keeps travelling; the citation that would prove who told it first does not.
context.pull: “Tentatively credited” is as far as the evidence goes — and further than most quote sites admit.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator investigated this quote; earliest citations are the Liverpool Echo, 5 January 1959, page 8, column 6, in 'Echoes and Gossip of the Day' under 'Settling Up' ('Money can't buy health. but I'd settle for a diamond-studded wheelchair. —Dorothy Parker.'), and the Nantwich Guardian, 19 February 1959; Evan Esar's 20,000 Quips and Quotes (1968, Doubleday, p. 374) prints 'Money cannot buy health...' under 'Health and Wealth'; a 1974 Circus magazine piece on Brownsville Station uses the diamond-studded wheelchair image; The Kansas City Times (1977) and The Portable Curmudgeon (1987) reprint it with the Parker credit; Barry Day's Dorothy Parker In Her Own Words (2004, p. 104) places it beside a 1956 Paris Review quote in which it does not occur and gives no supporting citation; QI concludes the quotation 'should be tentatively credited to Dorothy Parker' with no direct evidence from Parker's own writings.
Wikiquote's Dorothy Parker page contains neither 'diamond-studded wheelchair' nor 'Money cannot buy health' in any section (Quotes, Attributed, Misattributed, or the sourced work sections).

Dorothy Parker was born Dorothy Rothschild on 22 August 1893 in Long Branch, New Jersey and died 7 June 1967 in New York City; she was an American poet, critic and short-story writer, theatre critic for Vanity Fair from 1918, a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, a contributor to The New Yorker, author of Enough Rope (1926), a Hollywood screenwriter with two Academy Award nominations, and was later placed on the Hollywood blacklist. The page does not mention 'diamond-studded wheelchair'.
The Internet Archive holds 'Dorothy Parker in her own words', associated name Barry Day (editor), published by Taylor Trade Pub., Lanham, Md., 2004.
Project Gutenberg ebook 68353 is Dorothy Parker's poetry collection 'Enough Rope: Poems', originally published by Boni & Liveright, United States, 1926.
The Liverpool Echo is a newspaper founded in 1879 and published in Liverpool, Merseyside, England.
